content: Succinic acid, also known by its IUPAC systematic name as butanedioic acid and historically referred to as spirit of amber, is a dicarboxylic acid that plays a critical biochemical role in the citric acid cycle. At room temperature, pure succinic acid exists as a solid, forming colorless and odorless crystals. It has a melting point of 185°C and a boiling point of 235°C. Succinic acid is classified as a diprotic acid, meaning it can donate two protons. The carboxylate anion derived from succinic acid is called succinate, and its esters are referred to as alkyl succinates. Biochemically, succinate is an integral component of the citric acid cycle. It donates electrons to the electron transport chain through a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase, also known as Complex II of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC). This enzyme is a four-subunit, membrane-bound lipoprotein that facilitates the oxidation of succinate and the reduction of ubiquinone. Intermediate electron carriers involved in this process include flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and three iron-sulfur (Fe2S2) clusters located within subunit B of the enzyme. Notably, Mark Donnelly from Argonne National Laboratory developed a highly efficient strain, AFP 184, to convert raw hydrolysates from biomass into succinate. Historically, succinic acid, or spirit of amber, was obtained by pulverizing amber and distilling it using a sand bath. It was primarily used externally to alleviate rheumatic aches and pains and internally for treating chronic urethral discharges (referred to as inveterate gleets). From a safety perspective, succinic acid is both combustible and corrosive, with the potential to cause burns. It is harmful if inhaled, ingested, or absorbed through the skin. Direct contact with the eyes can result in severe damage. Proper handling precautions, such as washing after contact, are essential. However, in its nutraceutical form, succinic acid is used as a food additive and dietary supplement, and it is considered safe and approved by the FDA. Succinic acid can undergo oxidation to form fumaric acid, a reaction that is significant in both biochemical and industrial contexts.
